title: Causal Trade-Offs in Superluminal Extensions of Relativity. A no-go theorem
authors: Amrapali Sen, Matthias Salzger, V. Vilasini
abstract: Extensions of relativity that include superluminal reference frames have recently been proposed by Dragan and Ekert as a way to reconcile relativistic symmetry with quantum uncertainty. In this work, we develop a causal modelling framework to formally study this proposal and prove a no-go theorem demonstrating that a theory permitting superluminal reference frames can avoid superluminal signalling only if it severely constrains which spacetime regions are accessible to operational protocols, if the choice of reference frame has observable consequences or if free variables do not exist or their existence depends on the reference frame. Crucially, our result goes beyond the familiar intuition that superluminal transformations may lead to superluminal signalling; our no-go result shows that Dragan and Ekert's proposal of introducing objective uncertainty does not, by itself, eliminate this conflict. In fact, because superluminal signalling might instead be avoided by relaxing other fundamental assumptions in the presence of superluminal reference frames, the proposed objective uncertainty may not be necessary at all. Our results clarify the limitations of uncertainty-based resolutions and the causal trade-offs faced by superluminal extensions of relativity.
summary: This paper develops a formal causal framework to study superluminal extensions of relativity, culminating in a no-go theorem. It demonstrates that maintaining causality and operational consistency in such theories forces a choice among several fundamental assumptions, showing that simple objective uncertainty is not enough to resolve the conflict. The work clarifies the deep causal trade-offs inherent in modifying the structure of spacetime causality.
main_problem: The paper investigates the causal implications of extending relativity to include superluminal reference frames (SpTs) and seeks to prove a no-go theorem regarding the avoidance of superluminal signaling.
main_result: The authors prove that avoiding superluminal signaling requires abandoning at least one of several fundamental assumptions regarding operational accessibility, frame-independence, or free choice, showing that objective uncertainty alone is insufficient.
method: They develop a formal causal modelling framework, generalizing affects theory, to analyze the compatibility of operational assumptions (A0-A4) under superluminal transformations.
model_or_system: The analysis uses abstract communication protocols involving particle emission and absorption between two parties, comparing results across standard and superluminal reference frames.
key_observables: Operational correlations between spacelike-separated regions, causal ordering of events, and the existence of free variables.
important_parameters: The nature of the superluminal boost, the size of the operational laboratory regions ($\Delta x, \Delta t$), and the degree of required uncertainty.
main_assumptions: The core assumptions tested include operational correlation (A0), preservation of causal ordering (A1), prohibition of superluminal signaling (A2), invariance of probabilities (A3), and invariance of free variables (A4).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the communication protocol setup in different frames; Figure 2 compares local deterministic descriptions in different frames; Figure 3 applies the analysis to the communication protocol.
paper_structure: The paper systematically tests the mutual consistency of five key assumptions (A0-A4) within the causal modelling framework, leading to the identification of necessary trade-offs.
why_interesting: While focused on relativity, the rigorous framework for testing the consistency of fundamental assumptions (like locality or observer independence) is a powerful tool applicable to analyzing constraints in quantum field theories or quantum gravity models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Communication protocol. The coordinates in black represent our frame, while the coordinates in red represent a superluminally boosted reference frame (of let’s say Charlie) with respect to us.

Figure 2: A tachyon is sent from Alice to Bob. Dragan and Ekert [1] argue that for this to be consistent with relativity, no local-deterministic model of the tachyon’s emission is available on the absorber’s, i.e., Bob’s side. Under a subluminal Lorentz boost, the roles of emitter and absorber change. Thus, by (relativistic) symmetry, they argue there can be no local-deterministic model on Alice’s side either.

Figure 3: Claim A and claim B applied to our communication protocol. The coordinates in black represent our frame, while the coordinates in red represent a superluminally boosted reference frame (of let’s say Charlie) with respect to us.
